ocr.Q1(a):
Big Data refers to extremely large and complex datasets which cannot be stored, managed or processed efficiently using traditional tools like RDBMS. It is characterised by 3 Vs:
1) Volume - It is the huge amount of data generated every day, in terabytes and petabytes. Eg. Facebook stores billions of posts, photos and comments.
2) Velocity - It is the speed at which data is generated and needs to be processed. Eg. live UPI payment transactions, stock market feeds.
3) Variety - Data comes in different formats: structured (tables), semi-structured (JSON, XML) and unstructured (images, videos, sensor readings).
Because of these 3 Vs we need scalable, distributed storage and processing systems like Hadoop.
ocr.Q2(a):
HDFS stands for Hadoop Distributed File System. It is the storage layer of Hadoop which stores very large files across multiple machines (nodes) in a cluster.
Features:
1) Distributed storage - files are split into blocks (default 128 MB) and stored on different nodes.
2) Replication - each block is copied on multiple nodes (default replication factor 3).
3) Fault tolerance - if one node fails, data is still available from the
replicas.
4) Scalability - new nodes can be added easily to increase storage.
5) High throughput - suitable for reading large datasets in batch processing.
Advantages: runs on cheap commodity hardware, reliable, good for big files and batch analytics.
Limitation: not suitable for low latency access or lots of small files.
ocr.Q3(a):
HDFS follows master-slave architecture.
NameNode (Master):
- Stores metadata i.e. file names, directories, permissions.
- Keeps track of which blocks are stored on which DataNodes.
- Coordinates client read/write requests.
- It does not store the actual file data.
DataNode (Slave):
- Stores the actual data blocks.
- Serves read and write requests from clients.
- Sends heartbeat and block report periodically to the NameNode.
- Creates, deletes and replicates blocks as instructed by the NameNode.
Together they provide distributed storage: NameNode manages, DataNodes store.
ocr.Q4(a):
NoSQL (Not only SQL) databases are non-relational databases designed for flexible data models and large scale storage.
Key features:
1) Schema-less / flexible schema.
2) Horizontal scaling across many servers.
3) Handles semi-structured and unstructured data (JSON,
documents).
4) High availability and distributed architecture.
5) Fast performance for specific workloads.
Advantages over RDBMS:
- Easier to scale out on commodity machines, whereas RDBMS
mostly scale up.
- Data structure can change without altering tables.
- Better for huge volume and high velocity data.
However RDBMS is better when strong ACID transactions and complex
joins are needed, so the choice depends on the requirement.

3) Variety - different formats of data: structured (tables), semi-structured (JSON, XML), unstructured (images, videos, text).
4) Veracity - quality, accuracy and reliability of data. Data may be noisy, incomplete or uncertain, eg. fake reviews.
5) Value - useful insights and business benefit that can be extracted from data, eg. product recommendations.
These Vs show why big data needs special storage, processing and analysis tools.
ocr.Q2(a):
YARN stands for Yet Another Resource Negotiator. It is the resource management and job scheduling layer of Hadoop 2.x.
Components / functions:
1) ResourceManager - master daemon that allocates cluster resources to applications. It has a Scheduler and an ApplicationsManager.
2) NodeManager - runs on every node, launches containers, monitors their CPU/memory usage and reports to the ResourceManager.
3) ApplicationMaster - one per application, negotiates resources from the RM and manages execution and monitoring of the tasks of that application.
4) Containers - bundle of resources (CPU, RAM) on a node where tasks run.
Benefits: allows multiple frameworks like MapReduce, Spark, Tez to share the same cluster, better resource utilization and scalability.
ocr.Q3(a):
MapReduce is a programming model for processing large datasets in parallel across a cluster of machines.
Mapper: reads the input split record by record and converts it into intermediate (key, value) pairs.
Shuffle and Sort: the intermediate pairs are grouped by key and sorted, then sent to reducers.
Reducer: takes each key with the list of its values and aggregates them to produce the final output, which is written to HDFS.
Example - Word count: Mapper emits (word, 1) for every word. Reducer adds all the 1s for each word, eg. (data, [1,1,1]) -> (data, 3).
ocr.Q4(a):
1) Key-Value stores: data stored as key and value pairs, very fast lookups. Eg. Redis, DynamoDB.
2) Document databases: store data as documents in JSON/BSON format, flexible schema. Eg. MongoDB, CouchDB.
3) Column-family databases: store data in column families, good for large distributed and write heavy workloads. Eg. Cassandra, HBase.
4) Graph databases: store entities as nodes and relationships as edges, good for social networks. Eg. Neo4j.
Each type is suitable for different data and query needs.

ocr.Q1(a):
Main challenges of Big Data Analytics:
1) Data storage - datasets are huge (TB/PB) so storing them cheaply and reliably is difficult.
2) Data integration - data comes from many sources and formats (logs, databases, social media) and combining them is complex.
3) Data quality - records can be incomplete, duplicate or inaccurate, which affects results.
4) Processing speed - streaming data arrives continuously and needs real-time processing.
5) Security and privacy - data may contain sensitive personal info, so access control and encryption are needed.
6) Scalability - the system must grow as data keeps increasing.
These can be handled using distributed tools like Hadoop/Spark and proper data governance policies.
ocr.Q2(a):
Traditional data processing vs Big Data processing:
1) Data type - traditional handles mostly structured data; big data handles structured, semi-structured and unstructured data.
2) Architecture - traditional uses centralized systems / RDBMS; big data uses distributed storage and parallel processing on clusters.
3) Schema - traditional has fixed schema (schema on write);
big data allows flexible schema (schema on read).
4) Scaling - traditional scales vertically (bigger server); big data scales horizontally (add more nodes).
5) volume and speed - traditional suits GB level routine transactions; big data suits TB/PB and fast streaming data.
Traditional systems are good for transactions and reports, big data systems for large scale analytics. Choice depends on data size, speed, format and workload.
ocr.Q3(a):
MapReduce processes data in the following stages:
1) Input split - the input data stored in HDFS is divided into smaller splits, each given to a map task.
2) Map phase - each mapper processes its split in parallel and produces intermediate key-value pairs.
3) Shuffle and sort - all intermediate values with the same key are grouped together and sorted, then sent to the reducers.
4) Reduce phase - reducer aggregates the values of each key and produces the final output which is written back to HDFS.
Example: in word count, mapper emits (word, 1) for each word and reducer sums the counts to give the total for each word.

1) Social networks - store user profiles, friends and relationships (graph DB like Neo4j).
2) E-commerce - product catalogue and shopping cart data
with flexible attributes (MongoDB, Redis).
3) Content management - blogs and articles stored as flexible documents.
4) IoT - storing large volume of time based sensor readings (Cassandra).
5) Real-time analytics - fast access to frequently updated data like leaderboards and sessions.
The DB type is chosen according to data model, consistency and query pattern of the application.
